name: Retiplex
tagline: Retirement planning software for modeling savings, withdrawals and whether the money actually lasts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The engine underneath a retirement planner is not exotic: a cash flow loop over years, a return series, an inflation assumption, and a Monte Carlo wrapper that reports how often you run out of money. An agent can write that in one sitting, and for a single household with simple accounts it will be honest enough to make decisions with. What it will not get right is the tax and benefit plumbing: withdrawal ordering across taxable, tax deferred and Roth accounts, required distributions, Roth conversion windows, bracket and surcharge cliffs, Social Security claiming timing, and whatever your local rules add on top. Those rules change every year and the whole product value is somebody keeping them current. Build it to understand your own numbers, not to replace the version that gets patched every January.
coreLoopDIY: A local Monte Carlo retirement simulator: enter accounts, contributions, retirement age and spending, and get a success rate plus percentile balance paths you can tweak assumptions on.
requirements: Current balances per account type and rough contribution rates
Your own assumptions for returns, inflation and life expectancy
Willingness to hand enter figures instead of syncing accounts
whatYouLose: Maintained tax rules: brackets, required distributions, surcharge cliffs, state differences
Smart withdrawal sequencing and Roth conversion optimization instead of naive draw order
Account aggregation, so balances are typed in and go stale immediately
Social Security and pension claiming logic based on actual benefit formulas
Sanity checking by someone who has seen thousands of plans, and printable output you would hand to a spouse or advisor
moatNotes: The hard part is not the simulation, it is the annual grind of tracking tax and benefit rule changes and not being wrong in a way that quietly ruins someone's retirement.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the output is used to make irreversible decisions, and a homemade model is exactly as good as its worst assumption. People pay for the feeling that the tax logic has been checked, that the withdrawal ordering is not naive, and that the number on screen accounts for things they did not know to ask about. A DIY Monte Carlo tells you whether 4 percent works; a maintained planner tells you what your actual after tax spending looks like at 73 when distributions kick in. That difference is worth a subscription to anyone within a decade of retiring.
notes: Great weekend project for learning what drives your own plan, terrible foundation for a decision you cannot undo.
prompt:
Build a local-only retirement plan simulator. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry, no external API calls.

Stack, non negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, Recharts for charts, Zod for input validation. All state persisted to localStorage. Simulation runs in a Web Worker so the UI stays responsive.

Inputs, one editable form panel:
- current age, retirement age, plan end age
- balances split into taxable, tax deferred, and Roth buckets
- annual contributions per bucket, with a growth rate for contributions
- desired annual retirement spending in today's dollars
- other income streams: name, start age, annual amount, whether it is inflation adjusted
- expected real return mean and standard deviation, plus inflation mean and standard deviation
- a simple flat effective tax rate applied to tax deferred withdrawals, clearly labeled as an approximation

Engine:
- 10,000 Monte Carlo trials, one year steps, returns drawn from a normal distribution, inflation drawn separately
- withdrawal order: taxable, then tax deferred, then Roth
- a trial fails the first year portfolio value cannot cover spending net of other income
- report success rate, median ending balance, and the 10th / 50th / 90th percentile balance paths

UI:
- success rate shown large, with a fan chart of percentile paths by age
- a table of median year by year cash flow: age, spending, other income, withdrawal by bucket, ending balance
- sliders for retirement age and spending that re-run the simulation live
- a scenario feature: save named scenarios and compare two success rates side by side
- buttons to export inputs as JSON and the median cash flow table as CSV

Explicitly out of scope, and say so in a visible disclaimer in the app: real tax brackets, required minimum distributions, Roth conversion optimization, Social Security benefit formulas, state taxes, account syncing.

Ship a README with the assumptions listed in plain language and how to change them. Include vitest unit tests for the withdrawal ordering and the failure condition.
